vignette:
Priya is a seventy-year-old South Asian woman, divorced, who has worked for decades as a freelance photographer. She came to the clinic at the urging of her adult daughter, who had grown alarmed by the degree to which her mother had withdrawn from the world over the past two years. Priya's PCL-5 score of 75 placed her in the severe range, and from the first session it was clear that the trauma at the centre of her presentation was not recent - it stretched back more than six decades, to a childhood defined by sustained physical abuse at the hands of her primary caregiver.

Priya described her mother as a woman whose rages arrived without warning. The beatings were not isolated incidents but a recurring architecture of her early life - her mother's hand, a belt, occasionally a wooden spoon, always accompanied by a torrent of words that told Priya she was the cause, that she had brought it upon herself, that she was shameful and unwanted. What marked these episodes most viscerally in Priya's memory was the particular quality of helplessness she felt: she could not run, could not call for help, could not make it stop. She learned, early, to make herself as small and invisible as possible, and that lesson never fully left her.

The memories themselves are fragmentary and disobedient. When Priya tries to deliberately recall what happened - to sit with it, to examine it - she finds the material strangely inaccessible, as though the past has been locked behind frosted glass. Yet when the memories come unbidden, they arrive with a ferocity that strips away the intervening sixty years entirely: the same terror she felt as a child floods her body, her heart races, and she is briefly, completely, back in that kitchen. Alongside the terror comes shame - a deep, somatic shame that she describes as feeling dirty from the inside out. This quality of the memory, its resistance to voluntary retrieval and its violence when it surfaces involuntarily, is shaped in part by the appraisals Priya carries about what happened to her. She has come to believe that she belongs nowhere - not to the family that harmed her, not to the South Asian community that, in her experience, kept such things private, not to the American social world she has inhabited for forty years. This profound sense of displacement colours how she relates to her own past: the memories feel alien, unintegrable, belonging to a self she cannot fully claim, and that estrangement makes deliberate recall feel both impossible and threatening.

The appraisals that organise Priya's inner life are relentless. She is certain that she must remain on guard at all times - that people, given the chance, will harm or abandon her - and this hypervigilance is not abstract but lived. On assignment, walking through a gallery opening or waiting in a client's studio, she scans exits and reads faces with an intensity that exhausts her and has made professional relationships increasingly strained. What compounds her distress most bitterly is her conviction that the people responsible have faced no consequences. Her mother died years ago, unreachable and unaccountable, and Priya finds herself returning again and again to the question of why this happened to her - turning it over, seeking a framework that might make it bearable. These appraisals - of perpetual threat, of injustice without resolution, of belonging nowhere - press directly on how she manages herself moment to moment. She tries hard to control her emotions in sessions and in daily life, holding herself in a rigid composure that she believes is the only alternative to collapse. When distress rises in public, she covers her face with her hands, a gesture so habitual she often does not notice she is doing it. These strategies of suppression and concealment, however, keep her from processing what happened: the emotional control and the hiding prevent the kind of engaged, contextualised recollection that might gradually soften the memories' rawness, leaving them as vivid and unassimilated as ever.

Priya came to seek help, finally, after she found herself unable to complete a portrait commission - she had looked through the viewfinder at her subject and seen, briefly, her mother's face. She is most afraid that nothing can be changed at this point in her life. What she hopes for, tentatively, is simply to feel that she exists somewhere in the world.
